title: Why Diet Coke Prices in India Have Jumped More Than 10 Percent
excerpt: An aluminium can shortage triggered by the Iran conflict and tighter import regulations has forced Coca-Cola to replace its popular 300-ml Diet Coke can with pricier, larger imports — and some consumers are paying nearly triple.
body:
Coca-Cola has hiked the price of Diet Coke in India by more than 10 percent after the Iran conflict choked the supply of aluminium cans through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a Reuters report citing two people with direct knowledge of the matter.

The company has replaced its standard 300-ml can — priced at ₹40 — with a larger 330-ml can imported from Southeast Asia, now selling at ₹50. On a per-millilitre basis, that works out to a 13.6 percent increase. In some cities, a new 200-ml glass bottle variant is retailing for close to ₹100, nearly triple the per-ml cost of the original can.

  • Coca-Cola has effectively raised Diet Coke prices by over 13% per ml in India, switching from a ₹40/300-ml can to a ₹50/330-ml imported can
  • The aluminium can shortage stems from the Iran conflict disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, compounded by India's BIS certification rules for can imports
  • Diet Coke is uniquely vulnerable because it is sold almost exclusively in aluminium cans in India, unlike Coke Zero which also comes in plastic bottles
  • A glass bottle version has appeared in some cities at nearly ₹100 for 200 ml, while "Diet Coke parties" have emerged as a social trend around the scarcity

The Aluminium Bottleneck

Diet Coke occupies an unusual position in India's soft drink market. While most carbonated beverages — including Coca-Cola's own Coke Zero — are sold across multiple packaging formats including plastic and glass bottles, Diet Coke relies almost exclusively on aluminium cans. That single-format dependency has turned a global supply chain disruption into a brand-specific crisis.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which aluminium cans and raw materials travel to India from Gulf-region producers, has been severely disrupted since the collapse of an interim truce in the Iran conflict. Around 9 percent of global aluminium production comes from the Gulf region, according to DAM Capital, and Indian supply chains have been hit hard.

"We've been placing orders but have been told there is a shortage due to war."

— A Coca-Cola distributor, speaking to Reuters

Adding to the squeeze, India's Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification for aluminium cans, which became mandatory in April 2025, has slowed both domestic production and imports. Delays in approvals have tightened supply further at a time when demand is surging.

Why Diet Coke Is Bearing the Brunt

The aluminium shortage has hit all canned beverages, but Diet Coke has taken the hardest punch. It is the fastest-growing diet drink in India by a significant margin, according to a leading bottling partner quoted by the Economic Times. Sales hit ₹50 billion in 2024-25 — the brand's highest since at least 2021.

The shortage first surfaced in Mumbai before spreading to Bengaluru, Pune, and parts of Delhi-NCR. Consumers reported the 300-ml can disappearing from shelves or being sold at inflated prices — up to ₹70 in some Bengaluru and Gurugram stores, according to Outlook Business. On e-commerce platforms, bulk discounts that once brought the per-can price down to ₹32-33 vanished overnight.

The scarcity spawned a peculiar cultural moment: "Diet Coke parties," where pubs and social media influencers charged ₹800-1,300 entry fees for events offering access to the drink alongside music and alcohol, according to Reuters.

Coca-Cola's Workarounds

To keep shelves stocked, Coca-Cola has turned to alternative sources and formats. The 330-ml cans are being procured from Southeast Asia at significantly higher cost — imported aluminium cans from the UAE, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asian markets are running 25 to 30 percent above normal prices, according to multiple industry reports.

At least one Indian bottler has also rolled out a 200-ml glass bottle for a limited period. But at close to ₹100 per bottle — compared with around ₹30 for the old canned format — the glass version is hardly a like-for-like replacement, according to Alcircle, an aluminium industry publication. Glass production costs have also risen due to higher fuel and LPG prices.

Domestic can manufacturers, meanwhile, are operating at near-full capacity with limited room to scale up quickly.

Ripple Effects Across Beverages

Diet Coke is not the only drink feeling the pressure. The aluminium and packaging crunch has pushed up costs of plastic preforms used in PET bottles and glass bottle production. Brewers have approached state governments seeking permission to raise beer prices by 12 to 15 percent, according to Outlook Business. Even India's condom manufacturing industry, valued at $860 million, has been affected by disruptions in aluminium and petrochemical derivative supplies.

Coca-Cola's CFO John Murphy told Reuters in April that the company was working to resolve the can supply disruption and expected improvement "in the coming weeks." Three months later, the problem has not eased — it has escalated into a formal price hike.

What Comes Next

Retailers and industry analysts say pricing and supply conditions will remain volatile until aluminium availability and Gulf shipping routes stabilise. For now, consumers have been shifting to Coke Zero, which remains widely available in plastic bottles, or simply paying the premium.

For the Indian diaspora, the Diet Coke saga is a small but telling illustration of how distant conflicts reshape everyday consumer experiences back home. A drink that cost 41 U.S. cents a few months ago now costs at least 53 cents in its new format — and considerably more in glass. The ₹40 can, for the moment, has become a relic of a supply chain that no longer exists.
nri_angle: Indian diaspora members visiting home or sending care packages may find Diet Coke harder to source and significantly pricier than before.
